title: The smallest thing that could ship
excerpt: Every project I have finished got smaller before it got done. Here is the question I ask to make that happen on purpose.
content:
I have a folder of half-built products, and they all failed in the same direction. Not one of them was too small. Every single one was too big on the day I started, and I spent the following months quietly discovering that.

So now I open every project with the same question, and I write the answer down before I write any code: what is the smallest version of this that a real person would pay for or come back to?

The answer is always smaller than it feels

When I built Cutlass, the first honest answer was: a command that takes a folder and puts it on the internet. No config file. No plugins. No accounts. One command, one folder, one URL.

That took eleven days. The version I had been sketching for a month — the one with a dashboard, a plugin system and a team plan — would have taken most of a year, and I would have learned nothing until the end of it.

Cutting is not the same as compromising

The trick is to cut whole limbs rather than trim every one of them. A product with six half-features feels broken. A product with one complete feature feels deliberate, and people forgive an enormous amount of missing surface area as long as the part that exists is finished.

  • Cut every setting. Pick the default you would have recommended anyway.
  • Cut the account system. Ask who genuinely needs to be logged in on day one.
  • Cut the second use case. It is almost never the one that pays.

If the smallest version embarrasses you, it is probably the right size. Embarrassment fades in a week. An unfinished project follows you around for years.

What to do with everything you cut

Write it down and then genuinely forget it. I keep one plain text file per project called later.md, and I have never once shipped something from it in the first six months. Which is the point: it was never the thing standing between me and a working product.

The list is not a roadmap. It is a place to put ideas so they stop taking up room.

title: I stopped measuring my week in hours
excerpt: Tracking time made me busier and no more useful. What replaced it is one sentence written on a Friday afternoon.
content:
For two years I tracked every working hour, tagged by project, and looked at the chart on Sunday evenings. The chart was always reassuring and almost never true. A forty-hour week and a twenty-hour week produced roughly the same amount of finished work, and the forty-hour one produced considerably more code I later deleted.

What the hours were actually measuring

Time tracking measures how long I sat down. It does not know the difference between the afternoon I spent choosing a database and the twenty minutes that afternoon in which I made the decision. Both are logged. Only one of them mattered.

Worse, the chart rewards the wrong instinct. On a Thursday with three logged hours, the honest move is often to stop and think. The chart says: open the editor.

One sentence on Friday

What I do now takes about four minutes a week. On Friday afternoon I write one sentence in a file, answering: what is true this week that was not true last week?

  • “Halfmoon sends alerts to Slack, and two people are using it.”
  • “I understand why the importer is slow, and it is not the database.”
  • “Nothing. I read, and I fixed two bugs nobody reported.”

That last one is allowed, and writing it down is the whole exercise. Three of those in a row is a real signal — much realer than a chart showing thirty-eight diligent hours.

It changed what I start on Monday

The sentence is easier to write when the week contained one clear thing rather than five vague ones, so I have started arranging weeks that way. Not out of discipline. Out of not wanting to write “nothing” for a third week running.

The file is nineteen months old now. It is the only project record I have ever kept past the first month, and the only one I ever read back.

title: Notes on writing a CLI people keep
excerpt: Small command line tools live or die on the first thirty seconds. Most of what makes them survive is not code.
content:
I have written a lot of command line tools, and thrown away most of them. The two that people other than me still run share almost nothing technically. What they share is how they behave in the first thirty seconds.

Do the obvious thing with no arguments

Run the tool with nothing after its name and it should either do the thing it is named after, or tell you in four lines what it does. Not a wall of flags. Not an error.

$ cutlass
Building ./site → 41 pages
Uploading to fly.io
Live at https://rowan-notes.fly.dev

Every flag I have ever added was a small admission that the default was not confident enough.

Print what you are about to do

The scariest moment with a new tool is the second between pressing enter and finding out what it touched. Say the destination out loud before you write to it, and say the path afterwards. It costs two lines and it is the difference between a tool people trust and a tool people wrap in a shell script to be safe.

Failure messages are the product

Nobody reads your README. Everybody reads your error. A good one names what happened, what it was trying to do, and the single next move:

No site found in ./site
  cutlass expects an index.html at the root of the folder.
  Point it somewhere else with: cutlass ./public

Three lines. Compare that with a stack trace, which tells the user about your program rather than about their problem.

Be boring about output

  • Colour is for two states: fine and not fine. Anything more and it becomes decoration people learn to ignore.
  • Detect a pipe and drop the colour, the spinner and the progress bar without being asked.
  • Never clear the screen. The scrollback is the only record of what happened.

A CLI is a conversation with someone who is already halfway through a different task. Say the useful thing, then get out of the way.

The part that is actually hard

None of the above is difficult. It is just unglamorous, and it all lands in the last ten percent of the work, after the interesting problem is solved and the tool technically functions. That is exactly where I abandoned the other eleven.

title: Rebuilding my site for the fourth time
excerpt: Four rewrites, each one smaller than the last. The current version is a folder of files, and I think that is the end of it.
content:
This is the fourth version of this site. The first had a blog engine, a comment system and a tag cloud. The second had a headless CMS and a build pipeline that took nine minutes. The third had an animation on every section and a theme switcher nobody used, including me.

This one is a folder of files, some type, and one green line that fills in when you point at a row.

Each rewrite removed a job

Every version failed the same way: I stopped writing, because publishing had become a small piece of engineering work. The tag cloud needed tags. The CMS needed a session. The animations needed checking on four screen sizes before I could post two hundred words about a bug.

  • Version one taught me that features on a personal site are chores in disguise.
  • Version two taught me that a build step is a thing that can break on a Sunday.
  • Version three taught me that a design I have to maintain is a design I will stop updating.

What survived all four

Three things, which is a useful list because it took four attempts to find them.

The list of things I made. It is the only part anyone has ever mentioned to me. It has been on every version, in almost exactly the same shape.

Dates. Without them, old writing quietly pretends to be current. With them, a post from 2023 is allowed to be wrong.

A way to reach me that is not a form. An address in the footer has produced more real conversations than every contact form I have built for anyone.

The test for version five

There will not be a version five if I can help it, but the test is written down anyway: can I publish a post from a train, on a phone, in under five minutes, without a build finishing? Right now the answer is yes, and I think that is the whole design brief.

title: Pricing a product with one customer
excerpt: The first price is not a market rate. It is a question, and there is exactly one person who can answer it.
content:
Roster had one customer for its first four months: a physiotherapy practice with nine staff and a whiteboard they photographed every Friday. I charged them forty euros a month, which was a number I made up while writing the email.

The first price is a question

With one customer there is no market rate to find. What there is instead is a single, answerable question: is this worth more to them than the effort of switching back to the whiteboard? Everything else — comparables, competitor pages, value-based pricing frameworks — is a way of avoiding asking it.

Forty euros was too low, and I knew within three weeks. Not because they complained, but because they had started scheduling around it. When a tool gets folded into how a business runs, its price stops being about features.

What I would do differently

  • Start higher and discount loudly. A “founding practice” rate is a gift you can give once; a raise is a conversation you have to have forever.
  • Price the whole practice, not the seat. Nine people at five euros invites them to count heads and prune.
  • Put the number in the first email. Doing it later turns a product conversation into a negotiation.

One customer cannot tell you what the market pays. One customer can tell you whether you have built something a business would rather not lose, which is the only thing that matters at the beginning.

Raising it

I put it up to ninety-five in month five, told them plainly that the original number had been a guess, and offered to hold the old rate for a year if that was easier. They took the new one without pausing, and asked whether I could add holiday cover.

The lesson was not that I should have charged more, though I should have. It was that the price had been quietly telling both of us how seriously to take the thing, and I had set it while distracted.

title: Against the roadmap
excerpt: A public roadmap for a one-person product is a promise made by someone who has not met next year.
content:
I published a roadmap once. Four quarters, twelve items, a nice grid of coloured cards. Within two months it had become a list of things I felt guilty about, and within four it was a page I avoided linking to.

What it actually did

A roadmap on a small product does three things, and only the first one is good.

  • It tells people you have thought past this week. Useful, and one sentence can do it.
  • It converts every change of mind into a broken promise, including the changes of mind that came from listening to customers.
  • It makes the next six months feel decided, which is the exact feeling that stops you noticing the better idea in month two.

What I ship instead

A changelog, and one line about what I am working on now. The changelog is the honest half — it is entirely made of things that exist. The one line is a statement of attention, not of intent:

Right now I am making the importer fast enough to run on a Monday morning.

Nobody has ever asked me for a date after reading that. Several people have written to say the importer was slow for them too, which is the conversation the roadmap was pretending to have.

The one exception

If someone is deciding whether to build their business on your product this quarter, they deserve a straight answer about the specific thing they need. Give it to them in an email, with a real date and a real caveat. That is a commitment to one person, which you can keep — not a commitment to everyone, which you cannot.
